messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo is a 22-year-old HVAC technician who came to treatment months after an accident at work in which another person was seriously injured. He described the day in a halting, overly precise way, as if he had repeated it to himself so many times that the sequence had become worn smooth without becoming any easier to bear. He had been on a service call in a tight mechanical space, working alongside another man while equipment was being checked. What stays with Mateo is not a broad story but a set of moments that still arrive with punishing force: the stale industrial smell in the air, the sudden shift from routine concentration to something going terribly wrong, and the instant he understood that the other person had been badly hurt. He returns again and again to what he did not do quickly enough, convinced that there was one more step he should have taken, one more second in which he could have stopped it. What torments him most is the belief that he stood there and failed when it mattered.

In the days after the accident, Mateo tried to keep moving. He went back to jobs, answered texts from coworkers, and told himself that replaying the event would help him understand it. Instead, he found himself circling the details relentlessly: where he was standing, what he heard first, what his hands were doing, whether his body should have reacted faster. He would lie awake running through tiny variations of the scene as if some overlooked fact might finally explain how it happened. He had come to believe that his own body had betrayed him in the crucial moment. If his reflexes, judgment, or coordination had failed once, he felt he had no reason to trust them now. On service calls he began second-guessing ordinary movements, pausing before touching equipment, watching his hands as though they belonged to someone less reliable than he used to be.

As time passed, the memory did not settle into the past. It forced itself into his mind without warning, especially when he was not prepared for it. He could be driving between calls, stocking the van, or sitting in his apartment, and suddenly the accident was there again. Sometimes what struck him first was smell. When he thought of that day, or when something in a work environment resembled it, he could catch the same odor from the scene so vividly that for a moment he felt pulled back into it. He found this especially disturbing because the memory often seemed oddly detached, almost as if it belonged to someone else and not to him. He would know intellectually that it was his experience, but it could feel unreal and estranged at the same time, leaving him shaken and confused afterward.

At work, Mateo’s world narrowed. As an HVAC technician, he spends much of his day in back rooms, rooftops, crawl spaces, and mechanical areas where sudden noises and stretches of stillness are common. He became acutely uncomfortable in unusual silence. In a quiet utility room, when the normal hum cut out and everything went still, he would feel his chest tighten and brace for something dangerous to happen. If a smell, a certain kind of enclosed workspace, or a moment of silence caught him off guard, his body reacted hard and fast: pounding heart, tension, a rush through his stomach, a sense that he needed to get out immediately. Over time he restricted himself to a very small number of places where he felt even somewhat safe—his apartment, his mother’s house, and a couple of familiar worksites he had been to many times. Anywhere outside that small circle felt exposed.

He also began organizing his life around avoidance. He stayed away from dates connected to the accident, growing tense as they approached and making sure he had plans to be elsewhere or alone. More broadly, he started avoiding anything he thought might be stressful, not only at work but in daily life. He turned down difficult assignments, left decisions to others, and stopped going to places where he might feel pressured or trapped. The consequences accumulated quietly. Coworkers noticed that he hesitated over jobs he once handled without much fuss, and he worried he was becoming someone they would not recognize. He felt that way himself. The version of Mateo he carried in his mind was capable, steady, and useful under pressure; the person he now encountered in the mirror seemed foreign, diminished, and hard to respect.

By the time he sought help, Mateo was exhausted by the effort of managing his days. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic collapse but the realization that his life had become organized around staying within safe edges and mentally revisiting the worst moment of it. He is frightened that this is who he is now: someone who cannot trust his own body, cannot leave the event in the past, and cannot forgive himself for failing to stop another person from being hurt. At the same time, he still hopes there might be a way to be at work without feeling ambushed by silence, smell, and memory, and to see himself as recognizably Mateo again.
